Flaxman orcid: 0000-0001-6033-4713 corresponding: true email: abie@ihme.washington.edu affiliations: - department: Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation name: University of Washington address: "Population Health Building/Hans Rosling Center, 3980 15th Ave. NE, UW Campus Box #351615" city: Seattle region: WA postal-code: "98195" country: USA - name: Anders Alexandersson # TODO before submission: confirm affiliation wording, add full street address and ORCID affiliations: - department: Florida Cancer Data System name: University of Miami Miller School of Medicine city: Miami region: FL country: USA abstract: | **Introduction** … **Methods** … **Results** … **Conclusion** … keywords: [record linkage, entity resolution, simulated data, cancer registry, benchmark dataset, reproducibility, pseudopeople] --- ::: {.content-visible when-format="docx"} ::: {#author-block .cell execution_count=1} **Author affiliations** | **Abraham D. Flaxman** (corresponding author), ORCID 0000-0001-6033-4713 | Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington, Population Health Building/Hans Rosling Center, 3980 15th Ave. NE, UW Campus Box #351615, Seattle WA 98195, USA | Email: abie@ihme.washington.edu | **Anders Alexandersson** | Florida Cancer Data System, University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, Miami FL, USA ::: ::: ## Key Features {.unnumbered} - **What is unique:** a large, fully simulated, multi-file dataset for linking individual people, with cross-file ground truth (every record carries a `simulant_id`, so missed-match and false-match rates of any method can be computed exactly rather than estimated), designed to capture the record matching challenges faced by a Florida-scale cancer data system. - **Why created:** linkage software for cancer registries must be developed and tested on names, dates of birth, addresses and SSNs, which are exactly the identifiers that confidentiality rules prevent registries from releasing. - **Details:** a simulated Florida drawn from the 50\,518\,675 simulated people recorded as residents in the simulated 2020, 2030 or 2040 censuses, including a simulated registry of 5\,000\,000 records whose age and sex distribution is that of the cases reported by the Florida Cancer Data System, and researcher finder files of 500\,000 and 100\,000 records drawn from residents in 2040. - **Data linkage:** the larger finder file includes 100\,000 people who are also in the registry and the smaller finder file includes 20\,000. There is no overlap between the finder files. - **Main categories of data:** simulated person-level identifiers including name, date of birth, sex, street-address fields, SSN, race/ethnicity, and a diagnosis date on each registry record, carrying realistic synthetic noise (typos, nicknames, month/day swaps, blanks, duplications). - **Access:** direct download under a permissive licence with a DOI. # Background {#sec-background} … # Methods {#sec-methods} ## Generating simulated records with pseudopeople ::: {#cell-sample-demo .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pseudopeople as psp census = psp.generate_decennial_census() # bundled ~10k-simulant sample census.head() ``` ::: {#sample-demo .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: # Results {#sec-results} We describe the released files first (@sec-structure), then the people in them (@sec-population), the errors in their fields (@sec-errors) and how hard those errors make the files to link with exact rules (@sec-difficulty). ## Structure, contents, and where the data are held {#sec-structure} This data resource is a zip archive containing three comma-separated data files and a data dictionary, to be deposited on Zenodo under a DOI that will be minted before publication. The high-level characteristics of the files are described in @tbl-release: a simulated registry of 5\,000\,000 people and two finder files of 500\,000 and 100\,000 people. All three are drawn from Florida residents in the simulated 2020, 2030 or 2040 census, a pool of 50\,518\,675 distinct simulated people. The larger finder file shares 100\,000 people with the registry, 20% of its records, and the smaller shares 20\,000, the same 20% share; the two finder files share no people with each other, matching the overlap design described above. The data dictionary inside the archive gives each field's type, format, blank convention, source and the noise mechanisms that touch it. The deposit also carries a manifest of MD5 and SHA-256 digests (@tbl-release gives the MD5) and the configuration file that names every seed and design target, and the pipeline that built them is archived under its own DOI. A second build from the same configuration and the same source population, which is available on request (@sec-access), reproduced all three files byte for byte. ::: {#tbl-release .cell tbl-cap='The released files: rows, people shared with the registry, size and MD5 digest. Each data file has exactly one row per person. SHA-256 digests are in the manifest deposited with the files.' execution_count=4} | File | Rows | Shared with registry | MB | MD5 | |---|---|---|---|---| | `sim_fcds_benchmark_0.4.zip` | | | 235 | `a6f2fd6a75dd8877fbfbb1f79e1f2b83` | | `registry.csv` | 5,000,000 | — | 565 | `5828e720d951f0403342de62201cd8aa` | | `finder_500k.csv` | 500,000 | 100,000 | 50 | `6025e4065d9616864fc0519d31da211a` | | `finder_100k.csv` | 100,000 | 20,000 | 10 | `c7411f89e300d097726616632bd4ef79` | | `data_dictionary.csv` | 15 fields | | <1 | `5807608b54bb9b1a72cc65f6b1477c91` | ::: ## Population characteristics {#sec-population} The simulated registry closely matches the age and sex distribution of the cases reported to FCDS between 1995 and 2023 [@pseudopeople_issue205]. The agreement is within 0.041 percentage points in each of the 36 age and sex strata. 62% of registry records are people aged 65 or older at diagnosis and 4% are under 40; 48% are women. The finder files have the age structure of the simulated population's Florida residents in 2040 instead: 26% of the larger file are 65 or older, 43% are under 40, and 51% are female. By race and ethnicity, people in the registry are 64% White, 17% Latino, 12% Black, 5% Asian and 3% other or multiracial (American Indian and Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander, multiracial, and unknown), compared with 55%, 21%, 12%, 7% and 4% in the larger finder file. The two finder files differ from each other by at most 0\.3 percentage points on every share reported in this section. The three most common first names in each age group, printed at the ends of the bars in @fig-registry-age-sex, run from Liam\, Noah\, Oliver among boys under five to James\, Robert\, John among men of 85 and over, and from Olivia\, Charlotte\, Emma to Mary\, Barbara\, Patricia among girls and women. ::: {#cell-fig-registry-age-sex .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Who is in the simulated registry. Share of registry records by age group and sex, stacked by race/ethnicity. Dots are the age and sex distribution of cases reported to FCDS, which the registry was drawn to match, so they sit on the bar ends by construction. At the ends of the bars, the three most common first names in each group as they appear in the simulated registry file.](paper_files/figure-html/fig-registry-age-sex-output-1.png){#fig-registry-age-sex width=699 height=631} ::: ::: @fig-example-pair shows three of the 100\,000 people who appear in both the registry and the larger finder file, chosen to show three kinds of error, with every field that differs between their two records marked: a first name recorded as a nickname, with a swapped month and day of birth and errors in three further fields; an address altered in three fields beside a blank SSN; and a swapped month and day of birth beside a swapped pair of SSN digits. The two records of a pair are one census record noised twice, so every difference in the figure is an injected error and not a move or a change of name, a simplification weighed in @sec-discussion. ::: {#cell-fig-example-pair .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Simulated people as they appear in the registry and in the 500,000-record finder file. Highlighted fields differ between the two records, and the note names what the discrepancy looks like; the diagnosis date is a registry-only field. The two records of a pair come from the same census year, so every difference is noise rather than a change in the person's life.](paper_files/figure-html/fig-example-pair-output-1.png){#fig-example-pair width=686 height=760} ::: ::: ## Error structure {#sec-errors} @tbl-errors gives the error structure field by field: the share of values that are blank in the registry and in the larger finder file, against the blanking rate set for each, and, among the 100\,000 true pairs, the share of pairs whose two records agree exactly when both have a value and the share with a blank on either side. Agreeing exactly means the two values are the same string, character for character. The error structure of the smaller finder file matches that of the larger on every figure in the table to within 0\.8 percentage points. SSNs are blank in 20\.0% of finder records, the rate FCDS specified, and in 5\.68% of registry records against a specified 5%. The build blanked no registry SSN, so every blank there is a person who never held one in the source population, where coverage varies with age: 3\.8% of registry records for people under 40 at diagnosis lack an SSN against 6\.4% for people of 40 to 64, and the registry's ages are the ones with the least coverage, which is why its share sits above both the specification and the whole pool's 4\.18%. Blank SSNs vary by race/ethnicity: in the larger finder file 28\.9% of Asian and 23\.5% of Latino people's records have none against 17\.8% of White people's, and in the registry the shares are 21\.5%, 15\.2% and 1\.9%. Of the SSNs present in the larger finder file, 4\,001 (1\.0%) carry two adjacent digits swapped, and where a true pair has an SSN on both sides the two agree in 99\.1% of pairs. Names and dates of birth disagree more often than SSNs do. Among true pairs with both values present, first names agree in 93\.9% of pairs, last names in 96\.0% and dates of birth in 93\.4%, and each of these fields is blank on one side in about 2\.0% of pairs. Taken together, 79\.2% of true pairs agree exactly on first name, last name and date of birth, and 77\.9% have an SSN on both sides that agrees. Address fields agree in 97\.1% of pairs with both present and are blank on one side in 5\.9%; the unit number is blank for 94% of registry records, because most addresses have none, and street numbers are blank above their set rates because some source addresses carry none. Dates of birth are blank in 1\.0% of registry records and 1\.4% of those present do not parse as a calendar date (such as a month above twelve); 13 registry records carry a Doe-pattern name (John or Jane Doe); no SSN in any file is a single repeated digit; and 52 SSNs in the larger finder file, and none in the registry, fall in ranges the Social Security Administration does not issue. ::: {#tbl-errors .cell tbl-cap='Error structure by field. Blank shares in the registry and the 500,000-record finder file, with the blanking rate set for each field in parentheses (FCDS\'s specification for SSN and address fields, pseudopeople\'s default elsewhere); and, among the 100,000 true pairs, the share of pairs whose two records agree exactly when both have a value and the share with a blank on either side. Street and unit numbers include the blanks present in the source addresses, so they sit above their set rates.' execution_count=9} | Field | Blank, registry (set) | Blank, finder file (set) | True pairs: agree when both present | True pairs: blank on either side | |---|---|---|---|---| | First name | 1.0% (1%) | 1.0% (1%) | 93.9% | 2.0% | | Middle initial | 1.0% (1%) | 1.0% (1%) | 99.7% | 2.0% | | Last name | 1.0% (1%) | 1.0% (1%) | 96.0% | 2.0% | | Date of birth | 1.0% (1%) | 1.0% (1%) | 93.4% | 2.0% | | Sex | 1.0% (1%) | 1.0% (1%) | 98.0% | 2.0% | | Race/ethnicity | 1.0% (1%) | 1.0% (1%) | 98.0% | 2.0% | | Street number | 5.6% (1%) | 9.5% (5%) | 98.3% | 10.3% | | Street name | 1.0% (1%) | 5.0% (5%) | 97.1% | 5.9% | | Unit number | 94.2% (1%) | 94.3% (5%) | 98.2% | 94.4% | | City | 1.0% (1%) | 5.0% (5%) | 97.2% | 6.1% | | State | 1.0% (1%) | 5.0% (5%) | 98.0% | 6.0% | | ZIP code | 1.0% (1%) | 5.0% (5%) | 97.5% | 5.9% | | SSN | 5.7% (5%) | 20.0% (20%) | 99.1% | 21.4% | ::: ## Linkage difficulty {#sec-difficulty} Among the 5\,000\,000 people in the registry, 97\.0% have a first name, last name and date of birth that no one else in the file shares, 88\.8% have a unique last name and date of birth, and 81\.6% a unique ZIP code, date of birth and sex, while 47% share their full name with at least one other person. @tbl-ladder scores exact-agreement rules on the larger finder file against the key. Agreement on first name, last name and date of birth links 79\.2% of true pairs at a precision of 99\.81%, and the SSN alone links 77\.9% at 99\.97%. The two field sets FCDS's Procedure Guide requires a submission to carry [@fdoh_fcds_procedure_guide_2007] behave differently as exact rules: name, SSN and sex makes no false matches and finds 64\.7% of true pairs, name with month and year of birth and sex admits 4\,421 false matches, 5\.5% of the pairs it proposes, and either set finds 81\.5%; the two sets of FCDS's current Data Linkage Record Layout [@fcds_linkage_layout], which both require the full date of birth, find 71\.7% together with no false matches. Name and date of birth or SSN, the best simple rule, reaches a recall of 95\.4% at a precision of 99\.82%, and last name with date of birth alone falls to a precision of 71\.0%. ::: {#tbl-ladder .cell tbl-cap='Exact-agreement rules on the 500,000-record finder file, scored against the identity key. Guide rows are exact agreement on the field sets the FCDS Procedure Guide requires a submission to carry [@fdoh_fcds_procedure_guide_2007], and layout rows on the two sets of FCDS\'s current Data Linkage Record Layout [@fcds_linkage_layout]; neither is the registry\'s own matching procedure. Missed-match is one minus recall and false-match one minus precision.' execution_count=11} | Rule | Predicted pairs | True | False | Recall | Missed-match | Precision | False-match | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | First name, last name, date of birth | 79,360 | 79,206 | 154 | 79.2% | 20.8% | 99.81% | 0.19% | | SSN alone | 77,943 | 77,923 | 20 | 77.9% | 22.1% | 99.97% | 0.03% | | Guide set: name, SSN, sex | 64,708 | 64,708 | 0 | 64.7% | 35.3% | 100.00% | 0.00% | | Guide set: name, month and year of birth, sex | 80,889 | 76,468 | 4,421 | 76.5% | 23.5% | 94.53% | 5.47% | | Either Guide set | 85,944 | 81,523 | 4,421 | 81.5% | 18.5% | 94.86% | 5.14% | | Either current layout set (name, sex, date of birth, with SSN or with address) | 71,666 | 71,666 | 0 | 71.7% | 28.3% | 100.00% | 0.00% | | Name and date of birth, or SSN | 95,533 | 95,359 | 174 | 95.4% | 4.6% | 99.82% | 0.18% | | Last name and date of birth | 121,362 | 86,117 | 35,245 | 86.1% | 13.9% | 70.96% | 29.04% | ::: Without blocking the two files present 2\.5 trillion record pairs. Blocking on the full date of birth leaves 58 million candidate pairs and keeps 91\.6% of true pairs, the pairs whose dates of birth are present and agree on both sides (@tbl-errors); blocking on the first letter of the last name with the year of birth leaves 1\.23 billion and keeps 90\.7%. @fig-stratified splits three rules by the race/ethnicity recorded on the finder record. For first name, last name and date of birth the missed-match rate is alike across groups, from 20\.1% to 20\.9%, and the false-match rate stays below 0\.31% in every group. The SSN rule differs by group: it misses 34% of true pairs for Asian people and 29% for Latino people against 19% for White people, and the difference carries into the best simple rule, which misses 7\.0% of Asian true pairs against 4\.0% of White ones. ::: {#cell-fig-stratified .cell execution_count=12} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Missed-match and false-match rates of three exact-agreement rules on the 500,000-record finder file, by the race/ethnicity recorded on the finder record, with the number of true pairs in each group.](paper_files/figure-html/fig-stratified-output-1.png){#fig-stratified width=660 height=303} ::: ::: The 11 rules run in 3.5 seconds on the 500,000-record file with 8 threads on an eight-core allocation. The 100,000-record file gives the same picture: every rule's recall is within 0\.8 percentage points of the larger file's. # Discussion {#sec-discussion} … # Data Access {#sec-access} … # Conclusions {#sec-conclusions} …
